title: Advice to young drummers, rock and Saturday Night Live
summary: Asked how he would pass his knowledge to young musicians, Leeman says today's drummers lack bands to learn in, does no hard rock though he played on early rock records, and describes NBC musicians admiring his cymbals.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: There would be two bands there -- and we'd get the house band together because it was such a wonderful thing.
I want to hear you say this to the people of the future. Can I ask you a question? I know what a great feeling this was, because I am of this era, I

heard you and I know this. Now how do you feel about trying to share this with young people today, to give them a chance to ... how do you feel about trying to impart your knowledge to young people today that they might be able to do this? Do you meditate or do you feel like that you would try to -- since you've been so blessed with this beautiful technique of playing, do you have any kind of feel about trying to help young people today to understand what you are about?
Of course it's a different era, but I'm asking how do you feel about it.

I'm trying to explain it to you. Unfortunately, drummers that are coming along today -- now they're into a different bag, they don't have that sort of a group to coincide with, to lend to and add to, to the thrill -- but I'm sure they must get thrills playing the music that they play. What they learn in school at the universities, they have charts to play. Now when those bands have a good day, they must know the inspiration I'm talking about -- and this doesn't happen all the time, so they figure there must be good and better times, you know? All according to who they associate with. It's hard for me to draw the proper picture.
Now I don't play any rock -- though I made the first

rock and roll records that were made, as a studio musician -- "Rock Around the Clock," I was hired as a studio musician. But I don't have that feeling of hard Rock, and some soft Rock I enjoy -- but they don't play the music where you can -- it's a hard-core playing that drummers do today, the music that's being played.

Musicians come up to me now that are doing that Saturday night show, the Saturday Night Live thing, and I worked on it a couple times a year, the past couple of years, over at Eddie Condon's, who is right down the street from NBC, and somebody would say "My name is so and so -- Now how the hell do you play with a setup like that, those cymbals? Jesus Christ, man, how do you play them like that?" And I said, well, it was just a habit I'm into, and I've had them come up and say, we're doing a show over at NBC, and Jesus Christ, I didn't know anybody was around that was playing like you. Now, that's no ego.
I did a couple of schools, and that's what I was there for. We played the jazz concerts.
That's the question I wanted to ask.
